subject: Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?

messages.author: 936421b3b4e13565
messages.subject: Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
parts:
Hi folks,

I think I may have discovered some issues with the interplay between objects of type "ordered" and objects of type "vector" in stan. To show these issues, let's consider a simplified version of a problem I'm working on. Let's say we are trying to simulate data from an ordered hierarchical multivariate normal model. The model is:

for( k in 1:K){
y[k] ~ multi_normal(beta_0_k[k], Sigma)
beta_0_k[k] ~ multi_normal(beta_0, Sigma)
}

I feed the model deterministic values for beta_0 and Sigma, I draw the beta_0_ks and the ys. The beta_0 and beta_0_k objects are of type "ordered". However, in the example I had in mind, the y might or might not be ordered (ie I might allow noise to mess up the ordering at that level of the model.) Now if the y is declared to be of type "ordered" the model gives the output it should logically give. But if y is declared to be type "vector" suddenly the model gives completely crazy results for the y draws, almost as if I were drawing from a standard normal no matter how big I make Sigma or how far from zero I make beta_0. 

Attached is the simulation in R with the 2 stan models and the output in a .txt file.

Can someone familiar with the object types let us know why this is happening, and is there any way to allow y to be a vector type if beta_0_k is an ordered type?

Thank you all so much for your time and effort! I really appreciate it.

Cheers
Rachael

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
parts:
The types are very simple.

ordered[K] alpha;

means that alpha is constrained so that alpha[1] < alpha[2] < ... < alpha[K].
The actual transforms are in the chapter of the manual on transforms. So
you get the Jacobian included in the log density. alpha[1] = alpha_raw[1],
alpha[2] = alpha[1] + exp(alpha_raw[2], ...

But

vector[K] y;

is just unconstrained. So you shouldn't expect the results to
be ordered, even if you draw y from a multivariate normal with
ordered mean --- it'll come down to the covariance. Do some
simulations outside of Stan and you'll see how it works.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
parts:
This does not signal a bug in Stan. Stan just samples
from the densities you give it.

If you look at the densities for ordered vs. unordered
vector parameters, they're very very different.
The ordered version removes all unordered results and
renormalizes with the Jacobians of the transform. I'm
guessing this is the step that doesn't match your intuition
of things shouldn't be that different. The problem is
that it's a very very different posterior.

Here's a thought experiment to help your intuitions. Here's the
unordered case:

parameters {
vector[10] y;
}
model {
y ~ normal(0, 1);
}


mean se_mean sd 10% 90% n_eff Rhat
y[1] 0.02 0.02 0.98 -1.22 1.28 3584 1
y[2] 0.00 0.02 1.00 -1.25 1.33 3761 1
y[3] -0.01 0.02 1.01 -1.31 1.30 3941 1
y[4] 0.00 0.02 1.01 -1.28 1.29 3872 1
y[5] 0.02 0.02 1.02 -1.22 1.34 3838 1
y[6] 0.01 0.02 1.02 -1.35 1.32 3821 1
y[7] 0.00 0.02 1.00 -1.26 1.30 3946 1
y[8] 0.02 0.02 1.00 -1.28 1.30 3725 1
y[9] 0.01 0.02 1.00 -1.30 1.32 3779 1
y[10] -0.01 0.02 0.98 -1.23 1.26 3874 1



And here's the ordered case:

parameters {
ordered[K] y;
}
model {
y ~ normal(0, 1);
}

mean se_mean sd 10% 90% n_eff Rhat
y[1] -1.54 0.01 0.57 -2.30 -0.83 1738 1
y[2] -1.00 0.01 0.46 -1.61 -0.42 4000 1
y[3] -0.66 0.01 0.43 -1.22 -0.10 4000 1
y[4] -0.38 0.01 0.41 -0.90 0.14 4000 1
y[5] -0.12 0.01 0.40 -0.63 0.38 4000 1
y[6] 0.13 0.01 0.39 -0.37 0.62 4000 1

y[9] 1.01 0.01 0.46 0.43 1.61 4000 1
y[10] 1.53 0.01 0.58 0.84 2.29 4000 1

In the ordered case, the y[n] are the rank statistics and
look very very different than the unordered case.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
parts:
Thanks Bob! I think we are getting somewhere now. I agree maybe my intuition about them being "close" is off, but the output of the second model I showed is "off" enough that you can't then recover the parameters of the DGP if you fit the same model back to it for inference.

In the case you showed, at least the 2 vectors have roughly the same order of magnitude and the SEs are roughly similar. In the case I showed above, the unordered vector "y" output is on the wrong scale entirely (except in the first few slots of each vector). It's different from the underlying mean, beta_k_0 by more than an order of magnitude. This happens every time. Can that really be right? In this case y is not a good signal of its own mean! So we can't recover the beta_k_0 vector from seeing the y and that is seriously bad news for inference. :(

Maybe it helps to mention that if I then fit the same stan model to the output of the simulation with y declared as a vector, it never recovers the right parameters -- the inference model thinks the y's are drawn from a multivariate standard normal with correlation 1 across slots, when in reality y's are drawn from the beta_0_ks shown in the simulation and the Sigma matrix as defined in the R code I posted above. This is even when the variable types are kept consistent across the simulation model and the inference model. This is the real problem I'm trying to solve: I might get a non-ordered y due to a noisy estimation procedure or noise in the draw, but i know that there is a logical constraint on the beta_k_0 (ie the mean of y's sampling distribution) so that it must be ordered. I want to estimate that beta_k_0 from the y, imposing that it be ordered, even when I see non-ordered y. 

Perhaps this very unhappy result is occuring because the Sigma in my simulation has a positive correlation across the slots, so that the first "y" draw then traps the rest of the y vector down there? I guess that could be the problem, but the variation allowed by the Sigma is so much larger than what I see with the y output that it doesn't seem able to explain all of the result.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
parts:
If you run only one iteration, you don't get a draw from the
posterior, you get a random init with each parameter drawn
uniformly from (-2, 2) on the unconstrained scale.
It has nothing to do with the data. We then do adaptation
during warmup and only then start making draws from the posterior.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange/wrong results from using "ordered" type and "vector" type in same model?
parts:
I step away from my computer for a few days and everyone
goes crazy!  Let’s step back and talk about densities and 
constraints to help understand what’s going on here.

Typically constraints are hard and weird and often cause
confusion, so it’s easiest to start with an unconstrained
problem and only then think about applying the constraint.

For example, say we want to draw samples from a 1D
Gaussian.  In Stan we do that be defining a 1D Gaussian
density, N(x | 0, 1) as

parameters {
  real x;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(0, 1);
}

Now say we want to limit ourselves to just positive values of x. 
This requires that we cut away all negative values of parameter
space _and_ update the density so that the integral over just the
positive values is 1.  We could do this by throwing away half 
of our samples after the fact, but that’s just a waste of computation.

What we really want to do is map our constrained space to
an unconstrained space and sample there (imagine taking
the line [0, \infty) and stretching it to (-\infty, \infty) ).
This requires three things: we need to define the constrained
space, we need to map into the unconstrained space, _and_
we need to update the density so that we’re sampling from
the same distribution.  Fortunately in Stan this is all done in
one line:

parameters {
  real<lower=0> x;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(0, 1);
}

Behind the scenes the “<lower=0>” defines x to be positive,
maps to a new, unconstrained parameter x_tilde, and updates
the density by adding a corresponding Jacobian transformation.
All of this happens automatically so that your chains can sample
efficiently and you get your constraint exactly satisfied in the end. 
It’s really quite magic.

Unfortunately, all of this becomes much trickier if the density
parameters are themselves being sampled.  For example,

parameters {
  real<lower=0> x;
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  // marginal distribution for mu and sigma...
}

Ultimately this means that there is no unique way of defining
an “ordered multivariate normal”.  Just adding the ordered
constraint

parameters {
  ordered_vector[10] x;
  vector[10] Mu;
  cov_matrix[10, 10] Sigma;
}
model {
  x ~ multi_normal(Mu, Sigma);
  // marginal distribution for Mu and Sigma...
}

is just fine, but it allows Mu and Sigma to take values that
could generate unordered vectors.  You can also define other
models that constrain Mu and Sigma to avoid these values.
This is easy for Mu, which can be made an ordered_vector
itself, but much harder for Sigma as you’d have to figure
out what correlations are incompatible with orderings!

Finally, if the measurement doesn’t preserve the ordering
exactly then you can’t assume the data is ordered!  Instead
you want to model the corruption by non-ordered noise
explicitly,

data {
  int<lower=1> D;
  int<lower=1> N;
  matrix[N, D] y; // not ordered
}

parameters {
  ordered_vector[10] y_tilde; // ordered latent vector
  vector[10] Mu;
  cov_matrix[10, 10] Sigma;
  cov_matrix[10, 10] Tau; // corrupting noise
}
model {
  for(n in 1:N)
    y[n]' ~ multi_normal(y_tilde, Tau);
  y_tilde ~ multi_normal(Mu, Sigma);

  // prior distribution for Tau, maybe strongly concentrated
  // around the identity

  // prior distributions for Mu and Sigma, possibly
  // including constraints depending on what model
  // the user wants to fit!
}

I think that was the issue?  If not let me know.

On May 25, 2016, at 8:04 PM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:

Oh, I see! So I thought this was true with fitting but not with simulation, but of course now that you've told me otherwise I see that it makes sense that the simulation is happening the same way since we're using the same machinery. 

When I run each model for 1000 iterations and extract a draw from the "posterior" (discarding the warm-up) y looks pretty great when declared as a vector type and declared as an ordered type! The difference between the two is much smaller. So I guess the initiation must be different and that's what produced such a major difference. 

I think we have sorted this out and can call it quits on the thread. Thanks everyone for your help and your patience. 

On Wednesday, 25 May 2016 11:00:24 UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
If you run only one iteration, you don't get a draw from the
posterior, you get a random init with each parameter drawn
uniformly from (-2, 2) on the unconstrained scale.
It has nothing to do with the data.  We then do adaptation
during warmup and only then start making draws from the posterior.

- Bob
